questions.stem: The internal energy of a system is the total of which two types of energy of its particles?

options.text: Gravitational potential energy and chemical energy
Kinetic energy and potential energy of the particles
Nuclear energy and thermal energy
Elastic potential energy and kinetic energy

questions.explanation: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energy of all particles (due to their motion) and the potential energy stored in the bonds between particles. It does not include gravitational, nuclear, or elastic energy of the object as a whole. Temperature relates to the kinetic energy part, while changes of state involve the potential energy part.

questions.stem: When a substance is heated and its temperature rises, which component of internal energy is increasing?

options.text: Only the potential energy of the particles
Only the kinetic energy of the particles
Both kinetic and potential energy equally
Neither - the energy goes to the surroundings

questions.explanation: When temperature rises, particles move faster, so their kinetic energy increases. Temperature is a direct measure of average kinetic energy. The potential energy between particles does not significantly change when there is no change of state. During a change of state (flat section of heating curve), the potential energy increases while kinetic energy stays constant.

questions.stem: A block of ice at 0 degrees C is heated until it becomes water at 0 degrees C. What has happened to the internal energy?

options.text: It has stayed the same because the temperature has not changed
It has decreased because ice is more ordered than water
It has increased because the potential energy of the particles has increased
It has increased because the kinetic energy of the particles has increased

questions.explanation: During melting, energy is absorbed to break the bonds holding particles in their fixed positions. This increases the potential energy stored between particles. The temperature stays at 0 degrees C, meaning the average kinetic energy has not changed. The total internal energy increases because potential energy has increased, even though kinetic energy remains the same.

questions.stem: A cup of coffee at 80 degrees C has less internal energy than a bathtub of warm water at 40 degrees C. How is this possible?

options.text: It is not possible; the hotter object must have more internal energy
The bathtub has many more particles, so the total kinetic and potential energy is greater
The bathtub water is denser than the coffee
The coffee has lost all its energy to the surroundings

questions.explanation: Internal energy is the TOTAL energy of all particles. While each coffee particle has more kinetic energy (higher temperature), the bathtub contains vastly more particles. The sum of all their kinetic and potential energies exceeds that of the coffee. Temperature measures average kinetic energy per particle, not total energy. This is why a bath at 40 degrees C can heat a room more than a cup at 80 degrees C.

questions.stem: When steam at 100 degrees C condenses to water at 100 degrees C, what happens to the internal energy of the substance?

options.text: It increases because water is denser
It stays the same because the temperature is unchanged
It decreases because potential energy is released as bonds form between particles
It decreases because particles stop moving

questions.explanation: During condensation, gas particles slow down enough for intermolecular bonds to form. Energy stored as potential energy between the particles is released to the surroundings. The kinetic energy stays the same (same temperature), but the potential energy decreases as particles move closer together, so the total internal energy decreases. Particles do not stop moving; they still have kinetic energy.
